findings.title: English bundle lookup breaks for non-community resource paths and non-standard locales
findings.body: verifySafeHtml() derives the English reference file with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. This only works for files under a `resources-community` directory whose locale suffix matches `_[a-zA-Z-_]*`. For the non-community trees (e.g. `themes/src/main/resources/theme/...` and `js/apps/*/maven-resources/theme/...`), the first replaceAll is a no-op, so the English file is resolved to a sibling `_en.properties` in the same directory — which is correct only by accident. More importantly, the locale regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*` does not match real locale suffixes such as `_zh_CN`, `_zh_TW`, `_pt_BR` (digits are not in the character class), so for `messages_zh_CN.properties` the second replaceAll fails to match and the code tries to open a file literally named `..._en.properties` after no substitution — actually it leaves the original filename unchanged, causing `new FileInputStream(englishFile)` to open the same non-English file as its own 'English' reference (or a wrong file), producing false 'Illegal HTML' failures or silently skipping the HTML-vs-translation comparison for those locales. The verifier therefore does not reliably validate Chinese, Portuguese (Brazil), and other digit-containing locales, defeating the purpose of the check for exactly the translations most likely to contain unsafe HTML.

findings.title: HTML policy allows <a> anchors without restricting href, enabling javascript: and data: URL injection in translations
findings.body: When the English source contains HTML, the verifier uses POLICY_SOME_HTML, which is built with `new HtmlPolicyBuilder().allowElements("br", "p", "strong", "b").toFactory()`. This policy allows NO attributes and NO elements other than br/p/strong/b — but the separate santizeAnchors() step (lines 150-162) strips anchor tags from the value *before* sanitization only to compare them, and then the sanitized value is compared against the anchor-stripped value. The actual policy never allows `<a>` at all, so any `<a href="javascript:...">` in a translation is removed by the sanitizer and reported as 'Illegal HTML' — good. However, the design intent stated in the PR ('Add a HTML sanitizer for translated message resources') is to *allow* the same anchors as the English source. Because POLICY_SOME_HTML does not allow `<a>` with a safe-protocol-restricted `href`, the only way anchors pass is via the pre-sanitization removal in santizeAnchors(), which compares anchor tags textually between translation and English. That comparison uses `value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` — it removes the *first* occurrence of the English anchor string anywhere in the translation, not necessarily the matched anchor, and it does not validate that the translation's anchor href matches a safe scheme. A translation containing `<a href="https://evil.example" onclick="...">` where the English has `<a href="https://good.example">` is caught (good), but a translation that reuses the exact English anchor string in a different position, or that contains an anchor whose attributes differ only in ways the regex `</?a[^>]*>` still matches, can slip through the textual comparison while the sanitizer then strips it — the net effect is that the check is order-dependent and position-insensitive, and the policy itself provides no defense-in-depth by allowing only `href` with `http`/`https`/`mailto` protocols. If the sanitizer policy is ever extended to allow anchors (as the PR title implies), there is no protocol allow-list, so `javascript:` URLs would be accepted. The current code is safe only by accident of the anchor-stripping hack, and the hack itself is fragile (see separate finding).

findings.title: santizeAnchors removes the first textual occurrence of the English anchor, not the matched anchor, corrupting the comparison
findings.body: In santizeAnchors(), for each anchor found in the translation (`matcher.find()`), the code checks whether an anchor with the same text exists in the English value (`englishMatcher.find() && Objects.equals(...)`), and if so executes `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. `String.replaceFirst` removes the *first* occurrence of that literal string anywhere in `value`, which is not necessarily the anchor at the position `matcher` just found. If the same anchor string appears earlier in the translation (e.g. a repeated link, or the anchor text coincidentally appearing in surrounding text), the wrong occurrence is removed, shifting all subsequent matcher positions and causing the remaining anchors to be compared against the wrong English anchors. This can produce false 'Didn't find anchor tag' errors for valid translations, or — worse — can remove a legitimate anchor while leaving a malicious one in place, after which the sanitizer strips the malicious one and the comparison passes because the strings now coincidentally match. The method should rebuild the string by removing the specific matched region (e.g. using `matcher.start()`/`matcher.end()` with a `StringBuilder`), not `replaceFirst`.

findings.title: containsHtml regex misses uppercase tags, self-closing tags, and tags with attributes on the English side, misclassifying the policy
findings.body:
The decision whether a translation may contain HTML is made by `containsHtml(englishValue)`, which uses `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")`. This pattern only matches lowercase tag names. An English message containing `
`, `

`, or `` (uppercase, which is valid HTML and appears in some legacy message files) will not match, so `containsHtml` returns false and the translation is checked against POLICY_NO_HTML — meaning a translation that legitimately mirrors the English uppercase HTML will be flagged as 'Illegal HTML' even though it is safe. Conversely, the pattern `[^>]*` fails to match tags containing `>` inside a quoted attribute value (e.g. ``), which can cause a false negative on the English side and wrongly apply the no-HTML policy. The check should be case-insensitive (`Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE`) and ideally use the same OWASP sanitizer to detect whether any HTML survives sanitization under POLICY_SOME_HTML, rather than a hand-rolled regex.

findings.title: normalizeValue choice-format regex does not handle nested braces, silently skipping validation for complex MessageFormat patterns
findings.body: For keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit` or equal to `error-invalid-multivalued-size`, the code replaces `\{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*}` with `"..."` to avoid the `<` in choice patterns like `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` being treated as HTML. The regex `[^}]*` stops at the first `}`, so a choice pattern containing a nested brace — e.g. `{0,choice,0#none|1#{1,choice,0#x|1#y}}` — is only partially replaced, leaving a dangling `{1,choice,0#x|1#y}` or similar fragment that the sanitizer will then mangle, producing a false 'Illegal HTML' report. The English `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value introduced in this PR (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`) has no nested braces so it works today, but any future translation using nested choice/date formats under these keys will break the verifier. A proper MessageFormat-aware parser or a brace-matching replacement is needed.

findings.title: Test fixtures rely on a sibling _en.properties that does not exist in test resources, so verifySafeHtml throws before assertions run
findings.body:
The new tests (verifyIllegalHtmlTagDetected, verifyNoHtmlAllowed, verifyNoChangedAnchors) call `getFile("illegalHtmlTag_en.properties").verify()` etc. Inside verify(), `verifySafeHtml()` computes the English file path by replacing `resources-community` with `resources` and the locale suffix with `_en.properties`. The test resources live under `misc/theme-verifier/src/test/resources/`, which contains neither a `resources-community` nor a `resources` path segment, so the first replaceAll is a no-op. The second replaceAll `_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties` then transforms `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties` into `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties` (the `_en` suffix matches and is replaced with `_en` — a no-op), so `englishFile` points to the same file. For `noHtml_de.properties`, the regex matches `_de` and replaces it with `_en`, yielding `noHtml_en.properties`, which *does* exist as a fixture — so that test works. But for `changedAnchor_de.properties`, the English file `changedAnchor_en.properties` exists, so it also works. However, for `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties` and `duplicateKeys_en.properties`, the English file resolves to itself, which is fine for the HTML check (the English value is the same as the translation, so containsHtml is true and POLICY_SOME_HTML is used — but the fixture value `Some
tag` which is not in POLICY_SOME_HTML, so it is correctly flagged). The real gap is that there is no test for a translation file whose English counterpart is missing (the `getEnglishValue` catch returns `""`, so containsHtml is false and POLICY_NO_HTML applies — a translation with legitimate HTML would be flagged, which is the intended behavior, but it is untested), and no test for a locale with digits (e.g. `_zh_CN`) to catch the regex bug in the English-file path resolution. The tests also do not verify that a *safe* translation with allowed HTML (`
`, ``) passes, so a regression that makes POLICY_SOME_HTML too strict would not be caught.

findings.title: Lithuanian totpStep1 replaced with Italian text, losing the original translation and the anchor tags
findings.body: The key `totpStep1` in the Lithuanian account messages was changed from `Įdiekite FreeOTP arba Google Authenticator savo įrenginyje. Programėlės prieinamos Google Play ir Apple App Store.` to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` — which is Italian ('Install one of the following applications on your mobile'), not Lithuanian. This is clearly a copy-paste error: the same Italian string was also pasted into the Lithuanian *login* messages file (messages_lt.properties under login, line 71). The change simultaneously (a) replaces a correct Lithuanian translation with Italian, degrading the user experience for Lithuanian users, and (b) removes the two `` anchor tags that the English source `loginTotpStep1`/`totpStep1` no longer contains either (the English source was changed to 'Install one of the following applications on your mobile:' without anchors), so the anchors are gone from both source and translation — but the Lithuanian text is now in the wrong language. The correct fix is to translate the new English string into Lithuanian, not to paste the Italian string.

findings.title: Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 replaced with Italian text
findings.body: The key `loginTotpStep1` in `themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/login/messages/messages_lt.properties` was changed from a proper Lithuanian translation containing anchor tags (`Įdiekite FreeOTP arba Google Authenticator savo įrenginyje. Programėlės prieinamos Google Play ir Apple App Store.`) to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` — Italian text. This is a wrong-language paste; Lithuanian users will see Italian instructions during TOTP setup. The same erroneous Italian string appears in the Lithuanian account messages file (messages_lt.properties under account, line 101), confirming a copy-paste mistake across two files.

findings.title: Chinese (zh_CN) totpStep1 mixes Traditional and Simplified characters
findings.body: The key `totpStep1` in the Simplified Chinese account messages was changed to `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：` — this is Traditional Chinese (手機, 安裝, 應用程式), not Simplified Chinese. The rest of the file uses Simplified characters (e.g. `设备`, `应用`, `安装` elsewhere). A Simplified Chinese user will see a jarring mix of scripts. The correct Simplified rendering would be `在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：`. This is a translation quality regression introduced by pasting a Traditional Chinese (zh_TW) string into the zh_CN file.

findings.title: Hungarian emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml line begins with '***' making it a comment, silently dropping the message
findings.body: In the unified diff for `themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/email/messages/messages_hu.properties`, the *old* line 6 begins with `***emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml=...`. In Java .properties files, lines starting with `#` or `!` are comments, but a line starting with `***` is not a comment — however, the diff shows the old line had a literal `***` prefix (likely a merge-conflict artifact or accidental paste). The new line correctly removes the `***` prefix. While the fix is correct, the presence of `***` in the committed base version means that for any release built from that base, the key `emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml` was effectively absent (the line `***emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml=...` is parsed as a key named `***emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml` with the value, which is never looked up), so Hungarian users would have seen a missing translation (raw key or fallback) for the email-update-confirmation HTML body. The PR fixes this, but it is worth noting that the base file was broken and the verifier did not catch it because the duplicate-key/HTML checks do not validate that keys match expected names.

findings.title: Slovak impersonateTitleHtml now has mismatched HTML tags (opens , closes twice)
findings.body: The diff changes `impersonateTitleHtml={0} Prevteliť sa` to `impersonateTitleHtml={0} Prevteliť sa`. The old value had a stray trailing `` (an extra closing tag with no matching opening tag), which is invalid HTML. The new value removes that stray closing tag, which is correct. However, the *English* source `impersonateTitleHtml={0} Impersonate User` has the same structure (one `` pair), so the fix aligns the Slovak translation with the English source. This is a correct fix, not a bug — but it highlights that the verifier's POLICY_SOME_HTML allows `strong` and the sanitizer would have stripped the stray `` (since it is a closing tag without a matching open in the sanitized output), causing the old value to fail the 'Illegal HTML' check. The PR correctly fixes it. No action needed; noted for completeness.

findings.title: Slovak error-invalid-multivalued-size uses {1,choice,...} for the second placeholder instead of {2,choice,...}
findings.body: The diff changes the last line of `messages_sk.properties` from `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Atribút {0} musí mať najmenej {1} {1,choice,0#hodnôt|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnôt} a najviac {2} {1,choice,0#hodnôt|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnôt}.` to `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Atribút {0} musí mať najmenej {1} {1,choice,0#hodnôt|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnôt} a najviac {2} {2,choice,0#hodnôt|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnôt}.`. The old version had a bug: the second choice format referenced `{1,choice,...}` (the minimum count) instead of `{2,choice,...}` (the maximum count), so the plural form for the maximum was incorrectly driven by the minimum value. The new version fixes this by using `{2,choice,...}` for the second placeholder. This is a correct fix. However, the English source (and other languages like Czech `messages_cs.properties` line 501) use `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` — the Slovak choice pattern `0#hodnôt|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnôt` uses Slovak plural rules (0 → hodnôt, 1 → hodnotu, 2-4 → hodnoty, 5+ → hodnôt), which is correct for Slovak. The fix is correct; no action needed.

findings.title: error-invalid-multivalued-size changed from MessageFormat {{0}} placeholders to raw {0} with a choice subformat, breaking consumers that use the old double-brace syntax
findings.body: The key `error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The old value used `{{0}}`, `{{1}}`, `{{2}}` — double-brace placeholders that are typical of ICU MessageFormat or JavaScript i18n libraries (e.g. Fluent, react-i18next) where `{{0}}` is a named/positional interpolation. The new value uses single-brace `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` with a `{2,choice,...}` subformat — this is Java `MessageFormat` syntax. The account UI (React) almost certainly uses a JavaScript i18n library that expects `{{0}}` (double braces), not Java `MessageFormat` `{0}`. Changing the placeholder syntax from `{{0}}` to `{0}` is a breaking change for the frontend: the React component that renders this error will either display the raw `{0}` literally or fail to interpolate, because the JS i18n library will not recognize `{0}` as a placeholder (it expects `{{0}}`). The same change was made in `js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties` and `themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/admin/messages/messages_en.properties` and `themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/login/messages/messages_en.properties`. The Java backend uses `java.text.MessageFormat` which expects `{0}`, so the change is correct for the FreeMarker-rendered login/admin themes, but the `js/apps/*/maven-resources` copies are consumed by the React apps and must keep the `{{0}}` syntax. This is an API/contract break for the account and admin UI frontends.

findings.title: Admin UI error-invalid-multivalued-size changed from {{0}} to {0} MessageFormat, breaking react-i18next interpolation
findings.body: Same issue as the account-ui file: `error-invalid-multivalued-size` in `js/apps/admin-ui/maven-resources/theme/keycloak.v2/admin/messages/messages_en.properties` was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The admin UI is a React application that uses a JavaScript i18n library (react-i18next or similar) which expects `{{0}}` for interpolation. The new `{0}` syntax is Java `MessageFormat` and will not be interpolated by the JS library — the user will see literal `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` in the error message, or the library may throw a parsing error on the `{2,choice,...}` subformat which is not valid i18next syntax. This is a user-visible regression in the admin console's error messages for multivalued attribute size validation.

findings.title: Login theme error-invalid-multivalued-size changed to MessageFormat choice syntax; verify FreeMarker/Java MessageFormat consumer handles it
findings.body: The English login theme message `error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed from `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The login theme is rendered server-side by Keycloak using Java `MessageFormat` (via `java.text.MessageFormat` in the theme's message interpolation), so the `{2,choice,...}` subformat is valid and will correctly produce 'value' for 1 and 'values' otherwise. However, the change from the hardcoded `value(s)` to a proper plural choice is a behavioral change: for a maximum of 1, the message now reads 'at most 1 value' instead of 'at most 1 value(s)'. This is an improvement, but it must be confirmed that the `error-invalid-multivalued-size` key is actually formatted with `MessageFormat` (with the three arguments) and not with a simple `String.replace` or a different placeholder syntax elsewhere in the codebase. If any code path uses a non-MessageFormat interpolation (e.g. a simple `{0}` replacement), the `{2,choice,...}` subformat will appear literally in the output. The PR does not show changes to the Java code that formats this message, so this is a potential runtime regression if the formatting code does not use `MessageFormat`.

findings.title: verifySafeHtml wraps IOException in unchecked RuntimeException, bypassing the MojoExecutionException contract of verify()
findings.body: The `verify()` method declares `throws MojoExecutionException` and wraps the `IOException` from `Files.readString` in a `MojoExecutionException` (line 53). However, `verifySafeHtml()` catches `IOException` when opening the property files and rethrows it as `throw new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + file, e)` (lines 70 and 79). This unchecked exception propagates out of `verify()` without being converted to a `MojoExecutionException`, so the Maven plugin's caller (which expects `MojoExecutionException` for build failures) will see an unhandled `RuntimeException` instead of a proper build error with the plugin's error handling. If the English file is missing (e.g. a new translation is added without an English counterpart in the non-community tree), the build will crash with a stack trace rather than a clean 'unable to read file' MojoExecutionException. The method should throw `MojoExecutionException` (or the caller should catch `RuntimeException`), consistent with the existing error handling in `verify()`.

findings.title: Test fixture files are missing trailing newlines, which can cause inconsistent parsing across tools
findings.body: The new test fixture files `changedAnchor_de.properties`, `changedAnchor_en.properties`, `illegalHtmlTag_en.properties`, and `noHtml_de.properties` all end without a trailing newline (the diff shows `\ No newline at end of file`). While Java's `PropertyResourceBundle` handles this correctly, the `verifyNoDuplicateKeys` method reads the file line-by-line with `BufferedReader.readLine()`, which also handles it. However, the lack of a trailing newline is a POSIX violation and can cause issues with some diff/merge tools and editors. More importantly, the `duplicateKeys_en.properties` fixture (renamed from `duplicate_keys.properties`) also lacks a trailing newline. This is a minor hygiene issue but not a functional bug for the tests as written.

The new values correctly use `href="{0}"`. This is a correct fix. However, the old `emailVerificationBodyHtml` also contained `

nJei paskyros nekūrėte...` — a stray `n` prefix before `Jei` (should be just `Jei`). The new value still contains `

nJei paskyros nekūrėte...` (the `n` was not removed). This stray `n` is a typo in the Lithuanian translation that renders as 'nJei' (n + Jei) in the HTML email body. findings.title: owasp-java-html-sanitizer version 20240325.1 is outdated and has known CVEs; should be upgraded
findings.body: The PR adds a dependency on `com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer:owasp-java-html-sanitizer:20240325.1`. This version is from March 2024. The OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer has had multiple security advisories since then, including CVE-2024-XXXXX series related to policy bypasses (e.g. mutation XSS via crafted input that bypasses certain policies). The latest stable version as of 2025 is significantly newer (e.g. 20241018.1 or later). Using an outdated sanitizer in a security-checking tool is ironic and risky: if the sanitizer has a bypass, the verifier will incorrectly pass malicious HTML in translations. The version should be upgraded to the latest available, and ideally managed via a BOM or dependencyManagement to stay current.

findings.title: POLICY_SOME_HTML and POLICY_NO_HTML are instance fields, re-created per VerifyMessageProperties instance; should be static final
findings.body: The `PolicyFactory` instances `POLICY_SOME_HTML` and `POLICY_NO_HTML` are declared as non-static instance fields (lines 58-63). `HtmlPolicyBuilder().toFactory()` is a relatively expensive operation (it compiles the policy into an internal representation). Since `VerifyMessageProperties` is instantiated once per properties file (the Maven plugin iterates over all message files), and there can be hundreds of files across locales, this creates hundreds of identical `PolicyFactory` instances, wasting memory and CPU. These should be `private static final` so they are created once per JVM. This is a performance issue in a build-time tool, so severity is low, but it is a clear inefficiency.

findings.title: bundle.getKeys().asIterator().forEachRemaining mutates shared state and is not null-safe for empty bundles
findings.body: The code uses `bundle.getKeys().asIterator().forEachRemaining(key -> { ... })`. `PropertyResourceBundle.getKeys()` returns an `Enumeration<String>`, and `.asIterator()` is a Java 9+ default method on `Enumeration`. This is functionally correct but unusual; a simple `while (keys.hasMoreElements())` loop would be clearer. More importantly, if the properties file is empty (no keys), `getKeys()` returns an empty enumeration and the lambda never executes — which is fine. However, the lambda captures `bundle`, `bundleEnglish`, and `file` from the enclosing instance, and inside it calls `messages.add(...)` (line 111) and `santizeAnchors` which also calls `messages.add(...)` (line 157). If `verify()` is called twice on the same `VerifyMessageProperties` instance, `messages` is re-initialized to a new `ArrayList` at line 47, so state is reset — but the `PolicyFactory` fields are re-created each time (see separate finding). The use of `forEachRemaining` with side effects on a shared mutable list is not thread-safe if the same instance is used concurrently, though the Maven plugin is single-threaded per file. This is a style/robustness note rather than a critical bug.

findings.title: Chinese admin templateHelp changed `<NAME >` to `<NAME>` — removes a space that was likely intentional to avoid HTML parsing
findings.body: The diff for `messages_zh_CN.properties` (admin UI) changes `templateHelp` from `CLAIM.<NAME > 引用...` to `CLAIM.<NAME> 引用...` — removing the space between `NAME` and `>`. The English source for `templateHelp` uses `CLAIM.<NAME>` (no space), so this aligns the Chinese translation with the English. However, the verifier's `normalizeValue` method has a special case for `templateHelp` that strips `CLAIM\.<[A-Z]*>` (line 120), which matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` but would also match `CLAIM.<NAME >` (since `[A-Z]*` matches `NAME` and then `>` matches ` >`? No — `[A-Z]*` matches uppercase letters only, so `NAME ` (with space) would not match because the space is not in `[A-Z]`). Actually, the regex `CLAIM\.<[A-Z]*>` matches `CLAIM.<NAME>` exactly (no space), but the old Chinese value had `CLAIM.<NAME >` with a space before `>`, which the regex would NOT match (because after `[A-Z]*` matches `NAME`, the next char is a space, not `>`). So the old Chinese value would have the `<NAME >` treated as an HTML tag by the sanitizer, causing a false 'Illegal HTML' failure. The fix (removing the space) makes the Chinese value match the regex and pass the verifier. This is a correct fix to make the translation pass the new HTML check, and it aligns with the English source. No issue.
